questions.question: What is an embedded server in Spring Boot and why is it useful?
questions.title: Spring Boot embedded server explained
questions.direct_answer: An embedded server is a web server (Tomcat by default) that is bundled inside your application JAR and starts with it. Unlike traditional deployment where you deploy a WAR to a separately installed Tomcat, the embedded server means your app is self-contained — run java -jar and both the app and server start together.
questions.interviewer_intent: Embedded server is one of Spring Boot's defining features — test whether the candidate understands the deployment model shift.

sections.content: Before Spring Boot, Java web deployment meant: install Tomcat separately on the server, build a WAR file, put it in Tomcat's webapps directory, configure Tomcat's server.xml. Your application and the server were two separate things. Spring Boot changed this by including Tomcat as a regular Maven dependency. When your app starts, it spins up an embedded Tomcat internally, deploys itself to it, and starts accepting requests. The server is just another library. This model is what makes Docker-based microservices so clean — one container, one JAR, one java -jar command. No server configuration files, no deploy steps.

# Traditional deployment
mvn package
cp target/myapp.war /opt/tomcat/webapps/
/opt/tomcat/bin/startup.sh

# Spring Boot embedded server
mvn package
java -jar target/myapp.jar  # server starts with the app
Embedded = server is a library, not a separate installation. Self-contained JAR is the Spring Boot deployment unit.

questions.question: What embedded servers does Spring Boot support and how do you switch between them?
questions.title: Tomcat vs Jetty vs Undertow in Spring Boot
questions.direct_answer: Spring Boot supports Tomcat (default), Jetty, and Undertow. To switch, exclude spring-boot-starter-tomcat from spring-boot-starter-web and add the desired server's starter. All three are production-ready; Tomcat has the largest community, Undertow is lightweight with good performance, Jetty is a good middle ground.
questions.interviewer_intent: Practical knowledge of server options — shows the candidate understands Spring Boot's pluggable server model.

sections.content: All three are fully supported and interchangeable. Tomcat is the default — largest community, most documentation, well-understood in the industry. Jetty is popular in environments where memory footprint matters. Undertow is a newer option from JBoss that performs well under load. Switching is an exclusion-plus-addition pattern in Maven. For the vast majority of business applications the choice is irrelevant — pick Tomcat and move on. The choice matters more for high-performance services handling thousands of concurrent requests per second.

<!-- Switch to Undertow -->
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
  <exclusions>
    <exclusion>
      <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
      <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-tomcat</artifactId>
    </exclusion>
  </exclusions>
</dependency>
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-undertow</artifactId>
</dependency>

questions.question: How do you configure the embedded Tomcat in Spring Boot?
questions.title: Configuring embedded Tomcat — port, threads, timeout
questions.direct_answer: Configure embedded Tomcat via server.* properties in application.properties. Key properties: server.port (default 8080), server.tomcat.threads.max (max worker threads, default 200), server.tomcat.connection-timeout, server.tomcat.max-connections. For advanced configuration, define a WebServerFactoryCustomizer bean.
questions.interviewer_intent: Tests knowledge beyond just running the server — can the candidate tune it for production?

sections.content: Most Tomcat settings are exposed as server properties. The common ones you'll tune: server.port for the port. server.tomcat.threads.max for the maximum thread pool size — default is 200, meaning up to 200 concurrent requests handled simultaneously. For high-traffic services you might increase this. server.tomcat.connection-timeout for how long Tomcat waits for a client to send data. For settings not exposed as properties, Spring Boot provides WebServerFactoryCustomizer — you implement it and get access to the raw server factory where you can set anything.

# application.properties
server.port=8080
server.tomcat.threads.max=300
server.tomcat.threads.min-spare=10
server.tomcat.connection-timeout=30s
server.tomcat.max-connections=10000
server.tomcat.threads.max=200 is the default. For high-load apps, tune this based on hardware and expected concurrency.

questions.question: How do you configure HTTPS for the Spring Boot embedded server?
questions.title: HTTPS configuration in Spring Boot
questions.direct_answer: Configure HTTPS by setting server.ssl.key-store, server.ssl.key-store-password, and server.ssl.key-store-type in application.properties, pointing to a keystore containing your certificate. Set server.port=8443 (conventional HTTPS port). For local development, generate a self-signed certificate with keytool or use Spring Boot's built-in support.
questions.interviewer_intent: HTTPS is mandatory in production — tests whether the candidate knows the basic SSL configuration.

sections.content: Spring Boot makes HTTPS configuration straightforward. You need a keystore — a file that contains your certificate and private key. In production this comes from a certificate authority. For local development you generate a self-signed one with the keytool command that ships with the JDK. Then point Spring Boot at it via properties. server.ssl.key-store is the path to the keystore file, key-store-password is the password, key-store-type is either JKS or PKCS12. Change the port to 8443 by convention. In production you'd typically terminate SSL at a load balancer, so the Spring Boot app only handles HTTP internally — but knowing the direct SSL setup is still important.

# application.properties
server.port=8443
server.ssl.enabled=true
server.ssl.key-store=classpath:keystore.p12
server.ssl.key-store-password=changeit
server.ssl.key-store-type=PKCS12
server.ssl.key-alias=myapp
In production, SSL termination at load balancer (AWS ALB, nginx) is more common than Spring Boot handling SSL directly.

questions.question: How does the embedded server lifecycle relate to the Spring ApplicationContext?
questions.title: Embedded server and ApplicationContext lifecycle
questions.direct_answer: The embedded server starts after the ApplicationContext is fully initialized — beans are created and wired first, then the server starts accepting requests. On shutdown, the server stops accepting new requests, ongoing requests complete (graceful shutdown), then the ApplicationContext closes, running @PreDestroy methods and releasing resources.
questions.interviewer_intent: Tests deeper understanding of the startup/shutdown sequence — relevant for production reliability.

sections.content: The startup order is important for correctness. Spring Boot first creates all the beans and runs auto-configuration. Only after the ApplicationContext is fully ready — all beans created, @PostConstruct methods called, CommandLineRunners executed — does it start the embedded server. This ensures your application is ready to handle requests before the first request can arrive. On shutdown, Spring Boot 2.3+ added graceful shutdown support: you enable it and Tomcat stops accepting new connections immediately but waits for in-flight requests to finish, then the ApplicationContext closes and @PreDestroy methods clean up resources like database connections.

# Enable graceful shutdown (Spring Boot 2.3+)
server.shutdown=graceful
spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase=30s
Start: beans wired → server opens. Shutdown: server stops accepting → in-flight requests drain → context closes → @PreDestroy runs.

questions.question: Can you deploy a Spring Boot application as a WAR to an external Tomcat?
questions.title: Spring Boot WAR deployment to external server
questions.direct_answer: Yes. Change packaging from jar to war in pom.xml, extend SpringBootServletInitializer, and override configure(). Exclude the embedded Tomcat (mark it as provided scope). Build with mvn package and deploy the WAR to external Tomcat. This allows running Boot apps on enterprise app servers.
questions.interviewer_intent: Tests knowledge of the WAR deployment path — relevant for enterprise environments.

sections.content: Even though Spring Boot's default is a fat JAR with embedded server, you can package it as a WAR if you need to deploy to a company-mandated application server. The changes are: update pom.xml packaging to war, mark the embedded Tomcat as provided scope so it's not included in the WAR, and extend SpringBootServletInitializer and override configure() — this is the hook that the external servlet container calls to start your application. The WAR is then a regular deployable artifact. Modern Spring Boot apps rarely need this, but enterprise environments sometimes mandate it.
Extend SpringBootServletInitializer for WAR deployment. Mark embedded Tomcat as <scope>provided</scope> in pom.xml.

questions.question: What is context path in Spring Boot and how do you configure it?
questions.title: Spring Boot context path configuration
questions.direct_answer: The context path is a prefix added to all application URLs. By default it is / (empty), so endpoints are at /users, /orders, etc. Setting server.servlet.context-path=/api means all endpoints are prefixed: /api/users, /api/orders. This is useful when multiple apps are deployed to the same server on different paths.
questions.interviewer_intent: Practical configuration question — tests whether the candidate knows how to configure the application root path.

sections.content: Context path is the root path under which your application serves requests. By default it's empty, so a controller mapped to /users is accessible at /users. If you set context-path to /api, that same controller is now at /api/users. This is most useful when multiple applications run on the same server and need to be differentiated by path. In microservices with a dedicated server per app, you often leave it as default. Another use case is when an API gateway strips a prefix — your app's context path matches what comes through.

# application.properties
server.servlet.context-path=/api
# Now: GET /api/users instead of GET /users
server.servlet.context-path=/api adds /api prefix to ALL endpoints including Actuator endpoints.
